'''Robert Helmer MacArthur''' (April 7, 1930 &ndash; November 1, 1972) was a Canadian-born American [[ecology|ecologist]] who made a major impact on many areas of [[community ecology|community]] and [[population ecology]]. He is considered to be one of the founders of ecology.<ref name="Wilson">{{cite book |last1=Wilson |first1=Edward O. |last2=Hutchinson |first2=G . Evelyn |chapter=Robert Helmer MacArthur 1930—1972 |title=Biographical Memoirs |date=1 January 1989 |volume=58 |location=Washington, DC |publisher= The National Academies Press  |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/mac-arthur-robert-h.pdf}}</ref>

==Early life and education ==
MacArthur was born in Toronto, Ontario, to John Wood MacArthur and Olive Turner in 1930. He later moved to [[Marlboro, Vermont]], as his father moved from the 
[[University of Toronto]] to [[Marlboro College]].<ref name = "Odenbaugh 2011">{{cite book|last=Odenbaugh|first=Jay|title=Philosophy of Ecology|editor-last1 = Gabbay |editor-first1 = Dov M.|editor-last2 = Brown |editor-first2 = Bryson  |editor-last3 = Thagard |editor-first3 = Paul | editor-last4 = De Laplante |editor-first4 = Kevin |editor-last5 = Peacock |editor-first5 = Kent |editor-last6 = Woods |editor-first6 = John |publisher=Elsevier|year=2011|series=Handbook of the Philosophy of Science|volume=11|chapter= Philosophical themes in the work of Robert H. Macarthur|isbn=978-0-444-51673-2}}</ref><ref name="Odenbaugh 2013">{{cite book|last=Odenbaugh|first=Jay|title=Outsider Scientists: Routes to Innovation in Biology|editor-last1 = Harman|editor-first1 = Oren |editor-last2 =Dietrich |editor-first2 = Michael R. |publisher=University of Chicago Press|year=2013|pages=181–189|chapter=Searching for Patterns, Hunting for Causes: Robert MacArthur, the Mathemical Naturalist}}</ref>  MacArthur received his Bachelor's degree in mathematics from [[Marlboro College]], followed by a Master's degree in mathematics from [[Brown University]] in 1953.<ref name = "Odenbaugh 2013"/> A student of [[G. Evelyn Hutchinson]], MacArthur earned his Ph.D. from [[Yale University]] in 1957; his thesis was on the division of [[ecological niche]]s among five warbler species in the conifer forests of Maine and Vermont.<ref name=lack>{{Cite book|title = The Life of David Lack: Father of Evolutionary Ecology|url = https://books.google.com/books?id=jYFqXkWV8xAC|publisher = Oxford University Press|date = 2013-06-01|page = 203|isbn = 9780199339938|language = en|first = Ted R.|last = Anderson}}</ref> From 1957 to 1958, MacArthur worked as a [[postdoc]] with [[David Lack]].<ref name=lack />

==Career ==
MacArthur was a professor at the [[University of Pennsylvania]], 1958–65, and professor of biology at [[Princeton University]], 1965–72. He played an important role in the development of [[niche partitioning]], and with [[E.O. Wilson]] he co-authored ''[[The Theory of Island Biogeography]]'' (1967), a work which changed the field of [[biogeography]], drove [[Community (ecology)|community ecology]] and led to the development of modern [[landscape ecology]].  His emphasis on [[Statistical hypothesis testing|hypothesis testing]] helped change ecology from a primarily descriptive field into an experimental field, and drove the development of [[theoretical ecology]].<ref name="Pianka">{{cite book |last1=Pianka |first1=Eric  |last2=Horn  |first2=H.S. |chapter=Chapter 11, Ecology's Legacy from Robert MacArthur |editor-last1=Cuddington |editor-first1=K. |editor-last2=Biesner |editor-first2=B.|title=Ecological paradigms lost : routes of theory change |date=2005 |publisher=Elsevier Academic Press |location=Amsterdam |isbn=978-0120884599 |pages=213–232}}</ref><ref name="Fretwell">{{cite journal |last1=Fretwell |first1=Stephen D. |title=The Impact of Robert Macarthur on Ecology |journal=Annual Review of Ecology and Systematics |date=November 1975 |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=1–13 |doi=10.1146/annurev.es.06.110175.000245 |bibcode=1975AnRES...6....1F |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/doi/pdf/10.1146/annurev.es.06.110175.000245 |language=en |issn=0066-4162|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Wilson"/>

At Princeton, MacArthur served as the general editor of the series Monographs in Population Biology, and helped to found the journal ''[[Theoretical Population Biology]]''.<ref name="Rosenberg">{{cite journal |last1=Rosenberg |first1=Noah A. |title=Fifty years of Theoretical Population Biology |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |date=2020 |volume=133 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1016/j.tpb.2020.04.001 |pmid=32275891 |bibcode=2020TPBio.133....1R |s2cid=215733920 |url=https://rosenberglab.stanford.edu/papers/Rosenberg2020b-TPB.pdf |access-date=21 February 2023}}</ref> He also wrote ''Geographical Ecology: Patterns in the Distribution of Species'' (1972), which summarizes much of his life's work.<ref name="Wilson"/> He was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1969. Robert MacArthur died of [[renal cell carcinoma|renal cancer]] in 1972.<ref name="Odenbaugh">{{cite book |last1=Odenbaugh |first1=Jay |chapter= Chapter 10: Searching for Patterns, Hunting for Causes: Robert MacArthur, the Mathematical Naturalist |editor-last1=Harman |editor-first1=Oren Solomon |editor-last2=Dietrich |editor-first2=Michael R. |title=Outsider scientists : routes to innovation in biology |date=2013 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |location=Chicago |isbn=978-0226078403}}</ref>

=== The theory of island biogeography ===
Robert MacArthur, in collaboration with Edward O. Wilson, developed the influential [[Insular biogeography|theory of island biogeography]], which revolutionized how ecologists understand species diversity and distribution. Their seminal 1967 book, ''[[The Theory of Island Biogeography]]'',<ref>{{Cite book |last1=MacArthur |first1=Robert H. |title=The theory of island biogeography |last2=Wilson |first2=Edward O. |date=2001 |publisher=Princeton University Press |isbn=978-0-691-08836-5 |location=Princeton}}</ref> introduced the concept of a dynamic equilibrium between immigration and extinction rates as determinants of species richness on islands. They also coined the [[R/K selection theory|r- and K-selection theory]], which describes contrasting reproductive strategies: ''r-selected'' species maximize growth rates in unpredictable environments, while ''K-selected'' species emphasize efficiency and competition in stable environments.

Their equilibrium theory has been extensively tested and generally supported by empirical studies. For instance, researchers have validated the predictions regarding the effects of island size and isolation on species diversity through observations in archipelagos like the [[Galápagos Islands|Galápagos]] and experimental work on [[mangrove]] islands.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Simberloff |first1=Daniel S. |last2=Wilson |first2=Edward O. |date=1969 |title=Experimental Zoogeography of Islands: The Colonization of Empty Islands |url=https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.2307/1934856 |journal=Ecology |language=en |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=278–296 |doi=10.2307/1934856 |jstor=1934856 |bibcode=1969Ecol...50..278S |issn=1939-9170|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The theory also laid the foundation for [[metapopulation]] and [[landscape ecology]], broadening its influence far beyond island studies.

=== Niche theory ===
In their 1967 paper, MacArthur and Richard Levins formalized the concept of [[limiting similarity]], showing mathematically that there is an upper limit to how similar coexisting species can be in their resource use.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Macarthur |first1=Robert |last2=Levins |first2=Richard |date=1967 |title=The Limiting Similarity, Convergence, and Divergence of Coexisting Species |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2459090 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=101 |issue=921 |pages=377–385 |doi=10.1086/282505 |jstor=2459090 |bibcode=1967ANat..101..377M |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This work provided a theoretical foundation for understanding the conditions under which species with overlapping niches can coexist.

Earlier, MacArthur had demonstrated niche partitioning empirically in his groundbreaking 1958 paper on [[Warbler|warblers]] (''[[Setophaga|Dendroica]]'' species) in northeastern forests.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacArthur |first=Robert H. |date=1958 |title=Population Ecology of Some Warblers of Northeastern Coniferous Forests |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1931600 |journal=Ecology |volume=39 |issue=4 |pages=599–619 |doi=10.2307/1931600 |jstor=1931600 |bibcode=1958Ecol...39..599M |issn=0012-9658|url-access=subscription }}</ref> By observing how different warbler species foraged at varying heights and parts of trees, he provided one of the first clear examples of how [[Ecological niche|niche differentiation]] allows species to coexist.

MacArthur also contributed to the theory of [[Relative abundance distribution|species abundance distributions]] with his "broken stick model," first proposed in 1957.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacArthur |first=Robert H. |date=1957-03-15 |title=On the relative abundance of bird species |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=43 |issue=3 |pages=293–295 |doi=10.1073/pnas.43.3.293 |doi-access=free |pmc=528435 |pmid=16590018|bibcode=1957PNAS...43..293M }}</ref> This model likens the division of resources in an ecosystem to breaking a stick into randomly sized pieces, predicting the relative abundance of species in a community. While later models (e.g., the log-normal distribution) gained prominence, the broken stick model remains a landmark in the history of ecological theory.

=== Consumer-resource theory ===
MacArthur was a pioneer in developing mathematical models for consumer-resource dynamics, aiming to explain how interactions between species shape [[Community (ecology)|ecological communities]]. He introduced a general framework for consumer-resource interactions, which is widely used by theoretical modelers today and forms the basis of [[Coexistence theory|modern coexistence theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chesson |first=Peter |date=1990-02-01 |title=MacArthur's consumer-resource model |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/004058099090025Q |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |volume=37 |issue=1 |pages=26–38 |doi=10.1016/0040-5809(90)90025-Q |bibcode=1990TPBio..37...26C |issn=0040-5809|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He also used his model to demonstrate that increasing the number of species reduces a community's stability, a precursor to debates on the "diversity-stability" hypothesis.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=MacArthur |first=Robert |date=1970-05-01 |title=Species packing and competitive equilibrium for many species |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/0040580970900390 |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1016/0040-5809(70)90039-0 |pmid=5527624 |bibcode=1970TPBio...1....1M |issn=0040-5809|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

One of his key contributions was identifying a minimization principle for consumer-resource dynamics. He showed that these systems tend to minimize a quantity related to resource overlap, providing a theoretical foundation for understanding competitive exclusion and coexistence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Marsland |first1=Robert |last2=Cui |first2=Wenping |last3=Mehta |first3=Pankaj |date=September 2020 |title=The Minimum Environmental Perturbation Principle: A New Perspective on Niche Theory |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/full/10.1086/710093 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=196 |issue=3 |pages=291–305 |doi=10.1086/710093 |pmid=32813998 |arxiv=1901.09673 |bibcode=2020ANat..196..291M |issn=0003-0147}}</ref>

In collaboration with [[Michael Rosenzweig]], MacArthur helped develop the [[Rosenzweig-MacArthur model]] in the early 1960s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenzweig |first1=M. L. |last2=MacArthur |first2=R. H. |date=July 1963 |title=Graphical Representation and Stability Conditions of Predator-Prey Interactions |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/282272 |journal=The American Naturalist |volume=97 |issue=895 |pages=209–223 |doi=10.1086/282272 |bibcode=1963ANat...97..209R |issn=0003-0147|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This [[Predator-Prey|predator-prey]] model incorporates a [[Functional response|type II functional response]], where the predator’s consumption rate saturates with increasing prey density. Their model is notable for predicting [[Population cycle|population cycles]] in predator-prey interactions, which occur due to the lag between prey growth and predator consumption. This work remains central to the study of ecological dynamics.
